title: Fifteen Years to the White House
intro: He came back from Dakota a defeated mayoral candidate. Fifteen years later he was president, by way of a civil service desk, a police board, a navy department, a hill in Cuba, and an assassin in Buffalo. Fifteen questions on the climb.
heroAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as Assistant Secretary of the Navy
heroCredit: Theodore Roosevelt as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

badge.title: Fifteen Years to the White House

tiers.name: Civil Service Commissioner
tiers.line: Unglamorous, and you did the work.

tiers.name: Candidate
tiers.line: Third place is still a start.

questions.prompt: What was Roosevelt's first federal appointment, in 1889?
options: Collector of the Port of New York
questions.explanation: President Benjamin Harrison appointed him one of three United States Civil Service Commissioners at $3,500 a year — a small, thankless job enforcing merit hiring against a patronage system that had no intention of cooperating. He held it for six years, under two presidents of opposing parties, and made it noisy: he went after postmasters who sold jobs, testified against his own party's appointees, and treated a backwater commission as though it were a department of state.
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What job did Roosevelt take in New York City in 1895?
options: President of the Board of Police Commissioners
Comptroller of the City of New York
District attorney for New York County
Commissioner of public works for Manhattan
questions.explanation: He joined the four-man Board of Police Commissioners and became its president, taking over a force that was corrupt from top to bottom. His office was on Mulberry Street, and he ran the job as though the building were on fire.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt at his desk as police commissioner
questions.credit: T.R. at his desk as Police Commissioner. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What became Roosevelt's most notorious habit as police commissioner?
options: Riding patrol on horseback in uniform
Publishing officers' salaries in the newspapers
questions.explanation: He walked the beats between midnight and dawn to catch patrolmen off post, often with the reporter Jacob Riis. Plenty of them were off post — asleep, drinking, or sitting in a friendly saloon — and the ones he caught found the commissioner himself standing over them. "These midnight rambles are great fun," he wrote — and the papers loved them as much as the force hated them.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt in his Mulberry Street office as police commissioner
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt in his Mulberry Street office when he was police commissioner. The New York Public Library.

questions.prompt: Which reformer and photographer accompanied Roosevelt on those night walks?
questions.explanation: Jacob Riis, whose How the Other Half Lives had shown middle-class New York what its tenements looked like. Roosevelt read the book, walked into Riis's office and offered to help. They became lifelong friends.
questions.imageAlt: The New York City Board of Police Commissioners with Roosevelt at the centre
questions.credit: N.Y.C. Board of Police Commissioners, T.R. in centre. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Which unpopular law did Roosevelt insist on enforcing, to the fury of much of the city?
options: The Sunday closing law for saloons
questions.explanation: The law closing saloons on Sundays had gone unenforced for years and was used mainly to extract bribes. Roosevelt enforced it evenly, which made him briefly one of the most unpopular men in New York — and made the point that a bad law selectively enforced is worse than a bad law.
questions.credit: N.Y.C. Board of Police Commissioners, T.R. in centre. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: What post did Roosevelt take under President McKinley in 1897?
options: Attorney General of the United States
questions.explanation: Assistant Secretary of the Navy — a job he had said outright that he wanted. McKinley's advisers argued about it for weeks, on the reasonable grounds that Roosevelt would not stay quiet. He did not.
questions.imageAlt: Theodore Roosevelt as Assistant Secretary of the Navy
questions.credit: Theodore Roosevelt as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: In 1898 Roosevelt left Washington to do what?
options: Serve as military governor of Puerto Rico
questions.explanation: He resigned the Navy Department and helped raise the First United States Volunteer Cavalry — the Rough Riders — then went to Cuba with it, serving first as lieutenant colonel under Leonard Wood and then, when Wood moved up to a brigade, as colonel. Friends told him he was throwing away a career and leaving a wife who had just been gravely ill. He went anyway, and came home in August a national figure.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt and the Rough Riders at the top of the captured hill
questions.credit: Colonel Roosevelt and his Rough Riders at the top of the hill which they captured. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: What office did Roosevelt win in November 1898, months after returning from Cuba?
questions.explanation: Governor of New York, by a narrow margin. The party bosses wanted the war hero on the ticket and assumed they could manage him afterwards. That assumption did not survive his first year in Albany.
questions.imageAlt: Campaign poster for Colonel Theodore Roosevelt for Governor
questions.credit: For Governor, Col. Theodore Roosevelt; For Lieut. Governor, Timothy L. Woodruff. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Which New York party boss found Governor Roosevelt impossible to control?
questions.explanation: Senator Thomas Platt, the state's Republican boss, who had reluctantly backed Roosevelt for governor and spent two years regretting it — particularly over a tax on public-service corporation franchises that Roosevelt pushed through against him.
questions.imageAlt: Governor Roosevelt leading New York troops at the Dewey Celebration
questions.credit: Governor Roosevelt leading the New York troops, Dewey Celebration, New York. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

questions.prompt: Why did New York's party leaders push Roosevelt onto the 1900 national ticket as vice president?
options: He had lost his re-election bid
To get him out of Albany
They wanted him groomed for the presidency
questions.explanation: Thomas Platt and the New York organisation wanted him out of the governorship and into an office where he could do no damage, and the vice presidency was, at the time, exactly that: a political dead end with a gavel and no power. Roosevelt saw the trap and did not want the job. He took it anyway rather than fight his own party in public. Mark Hanna is said to have asked whether they realised there would be only one life between that madman and the presidency.
questions.imageAlt: Vice President Roosevelt at the swearing in of President McKinley, March 1901
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt at the swearing in of President McKinley, March 1901. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How long was Roosevelt vice president?
questions.explanation: Inaugurated in March 1901, president by September. He had time to preside over the Senate for a matter of days and to complain about how little there was to do.
questions.imageAlt: Vice President Roosevelt at McKinley's swearing in, March 1901
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt at the swearing in of President McKinley, March 1901. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where was President McKinley shot in September 1901?
questions.explanation: At the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, New York, on September 6, 1901, by the anarchist Leon Czolgosz. McKinley seemed to rally, then declined; he died on September 14.
questions.imageAlt: Vice President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during McKinley's illness
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during President McKinley's illness. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where was Roosevelt when word came that McKinley was dying?
questions.explanation: In the Adirondacks — he had gone climbing after McKinley appeared to be recovering, partly to signal to the country that there was nothing to fear. A guide brought the message up the mountain, and he came down through the night by buckboard.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt interviewed at Buffalo during McKinley's illness
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during President McKinley's illness. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: How old was Roosevelt when he became president?
questions.explanation: Forty-two — the youngest person ever to hold the office, and still is. John F. Kennedy was the youngest elected president; Roosevelt reached it younger, by way of an assassination.
questions.imageAlt: Vice President Roosevelt at McKinley's swearing in
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt at the swearing in of President McKinley, March 1901. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.

questions.prompt: Where did Roosevelt take the presidential oath?
questions.explanation: In the library of the Ansley Wilcox house in Buffalo, on September 14, 1901, hours after McKinley died. He wore borrowed formal clothes and promised to continue his predecessor's policies — a promise he kept for rather less time than his listeners expected.
questions.imageAlt: Roosevelt at Buffalo during McKinley's illness
questions.credit: Vice-President Roosevelt being interviewed at Buffalo during President McKinley's illness. Theodore Roosevelt Collection, Houghton Library, Harvard University.
